en: The Extensive Commentary on the Bodhicitta-śāstra, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Kamalaśīla.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master and Dharma-Transmitting Grand Master from the Western Heaven (India).

I take refuge in all Buddhas of the three times; Briefly collecting the various practices of the Mahāyāna, To establish this foremost and supreme undertaking, I shall now extensively explain the bodhicitta.
In this regard, how is it so?
If one wishes to swiftly realize all-knowledge, one should briefly summarize the mind by abiding in three points to give rise to compassion, and from that compassion, generate the great bodhicitta.
All the most supreme qualities of the Buddha-dharma have compassion as their root, and the cause of this compassion is the observation of sentient beings.
As it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*, at that time the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Bodhisattvas should not practice and study many diverse dharma-gates; rather, by diligently practicing a single dharma, they will obtain all dharmas as if from the palm of their hand.
What is this one dharma?
It is great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
When bodhisattvas rely upon this great compassion, they obtain all the Buddha-dharmas as if from the palm of their hand.
World-Honored One!
Just as wherever the wheel-treasure of a wheel-turning sage king travels, all power is gathered there, so too it is with the Bodhisattvas:
wherever their great compassion operates, they are able to accomplish the gathering of all the powers of the Buddha-dharma.
World-Honored One!
Furthermore, just as when a person’s life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is firm and stable, they are able to cause the various faculties (*indriya*) to function;

so too it is with the Bodhisattvas: because their great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is firm and stable, they are able to cause all the dharmas of the practices for enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*) to proceed.
As the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
you should know that the great compassion of all bodhisattvas is inexhaustible."
Why is this? Because it serves as the precursor for all phenomena. Śāriputra!
For example, just as the life-faculty of a person is preceded by inhalation and exhalation,
so too is the vast and universal collection of the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates, for it is preceded by the great compassion of the bodhisattva.
As stated in the *Gajapramardin-sūtra*, at that time a certain devaputra asked the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:
"How should one be able to initiate all the supreme practices of a bodhisattva?"
Furthermore, how does one abide?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Devaputra!"
Great compassion alone is able to initiate all the sublime practices of a bodhisattva.

Because a bodhisattva dwells taking all sentient beings as their objective sphere, they constantly give rise to thoughts of affection for all sentient beings, having no regard for their own person. They cultivate and benefit others with single-minded devotion, performing what is difficult to do over a long period of time, thereby giving rise to all [bodhisattva] practices.
As stated in the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*:
"Those bodhisattvas possess firm compassion; when they act to deliver all sentient beings, they do not harbor even the slightest notion of suffering;
and once they have delivered them, they likewise harbor no notion of having delivered anyone."

Without abandoning any difficult practices or ascetic austerities, one will thus before long bring all practices to perfection, fulfill original vows, realize all-knowledge, and attain all Buddha-dharmas; all of this has compassion as its very foundation.

All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have realized omniscience; with great compassion they universally embrace all beings, extensively bringing about the supreme benefit for the world, and abide in non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Such conduct of the Buddhas has great compassion as its sole cause.

Even when the Buddhas encounter suffering and affliction within the midst of their causal practices, they then direct their attention toward sentient beings, further increasing and intensifying their resolve without ever retreating.

As the Buddha has taught in various sūtras, all sentient beings undergo manifold sufferings within the various realms of existence, experiencing extreme anguish according to their respective conditions.

The Bodhisattva constantly observes sentient beings with compassion, seeing that within the realm of hell there are various sufferings: the fires of karma burn fiercely, and for long periods without interval, their anguish is inexhaustible.
Just as worldly thieves are subjected to various punishments— being bound, beaten, driven away with iron forks, having their limbs severed, and undergoing manifold sufferings—
so too is this suffering.

Within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), there are various forms of extreme suffering from hunger and thirst; their bodies are parched and withered, and for the sake of seeking food, they harm one another. Although they constantly search for it even for a hundred years, they ultimately cannot obtain even a small portion of discarded scraps, impurities, or anything else.
Furthermore, there are hungry ghosts whose own power is weak and inferior who rely upon others who possess superior power; although they do rely on them, they obtain nothing.

Even if they do obtain something, it is snatched away by powerful ghosts who deceive, humiliate, and oppress them, beating and punishing them, so that they undergo such immeasurable sufferings as these.
Those who undergo this suffering were formerly among those who possessed wealth, pleasure, and sovereignty; however, due to having committed various evils, they have fallen into this realm.

Within the animal realm, they endure countless sufferings: giving rise to thoughts of malice and harm, they devour one another; some have their noses pierced, others have their bodies torn apart, or they are subjected to beatings and bondage, utterly lacking autonomy. Their entire bodies are racked with agony, and there is truly not even the slightest portion of it that is pleasant or enjoyable.
It is like a person carrying a heavy burden who never tires; though it lasts for a long time, he does not think of weariness.

Furthermore, various animals in the vast wilderness roam about at will with single-minded abandon, galloping here and there without stopping even for a moment, harming one another and giving rise to mutual fear; within this realm of existence, there is yet such suffering.

Thus, in the various realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, because they give rise to various afflictions and evil karmas as their causes, they undergo all manner of suffering and distress within those respective realms.
Just as a person who has fallen into a steep and perilous abyss experiences suffering, so it is with them.
Within those realms of beings (*gati*), there are various sufferings as described in other places.

Furthermore, the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are scorched by the fire of desire, their minds are distracted, and they are unable to cause their own minds to be concentrated and gathered in one place for even a single moment.
One should know that when sensual pleasures perish, suffering immediately manifests; how could there be pleasure for one who is like a person suffering from poverty?
Within these heavens of desire, there is constant falling and destruction, fear, affliction, and ruin—none of which constitute true pleasure.
All the devas of the form realm are constantly subject to the flux of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
When their celestial retribution is exhausted, they may fall again into realms such as the hells.
Within these various realms of existence, beings are constantly bound by afflictions, karma, and the like, lacking any autonomy; it is from this that all forms of suffering arise.
Therefore, one should know that the fire of suffering blazes fiercely, consuming the world without ceasing.
Having perceived this suffering, the bodhisattva immediately gives rise to a heart of compassion and universally observes all sentient beings.

Furthermore, when the bodhisattva sees sentient beings undergoing various forms of suffering, he gives rise to a heart of pity and compassion—free from enmity toward some and favoritism toward others—and observes them with equanimity to deliver them.

Furthermore, since all sentient beings have been wandering in saṃsāra from time immemorial, there has never been a single being toward whom a bodhisattva has not conceived the thought of a kinsman or friend;
because they give rise to this mind of equanimity, they universally observe all sentient beings throughout the ten directions through such conduct.

If a bodhisattva sees a single sentient being who is suffering, they love that being as their own child and will immediately take the suffering upon themselves, so as not to let that sentient being undergo such suffering.

Because this compassionate mind is thus transformed, it can cause the suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings to be extinguished, thereby accomplishing the supreme practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
As the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:

"This practice of compassionate contemplation was first expounded by the World-Honored One in the *Abhidharma Sūtra*. Desiring to rescue and deliver all sentient beings, he gave rise to the power of compassionate vows and other such forces to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
If it were not for the sake of delivering sentient beings, I would never have resolved to attain this bodhicitta.
As the *Daśadharmaka-sūtra* states:

"Among all sentient beings, those who are without protection, without a refuge, without support, and without insight—when the Bodhisattva beholds them, he gives rise to compassion and thereby resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
If one does not provide guidance and instruction for others, a bodhisattva will not resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, it should be known that when bodhisattvas courageously resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is because their compassion is firm and steadfast.
As it is said in the *Tathāgatajñānamudrāsamādhirāja-sūtra*:
"The practice of the bodhicitta can destroy the suffering of saṃsāra.
And as it is said in the *Maitreyavimokṣa-sūtra*:
Good son, it is like a person who,

without relinquishing a great diamond treasure, separately obtains all manner of golden ornaments, yet does not abandon that great diamond treasure, thereby being able to universally relieve those who are impoverished.
Good son! It is the same for the bodhisattva:

without grasping the great vajra-jewel of the mind of omniscience, they may separately obtain the golden ornaments of the merits of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; yet they do not abandon those bodhisattva practices by which they are able to universally relieve all those impoverished by saṃsāra.
A bodhisattva is able to cultivate all trainings equally in every respect; this constitutes immeasurable and supreme practice.
Therefore, from the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) arises skillful means, which brings about the fruition of great enlightenment.
As stated in the *Tathāgatadarśanavijayasenarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"Great King!

Whatever various activities you perform, in every respect and in all places, you should train in them in conjunction with the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) up to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*)."
Therefore, Great King!

You should likewise give rise to a mind of aspiration, faith, seeking, and yearning directed toward the Perfectly Enlightened One; whether standing or walking, lying down or sitting, drinking or eating, or in whatever you do, you should constantly and resolutely maintain mindfulness and attention, visualizing all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.

Having gathered together all roots of goodness—past, future, and present—belonging to all foolish ordinary beings, oneself, and others into one place, and having given rise to a most exalted mind to rejoice in them, one should then share with all sentient beings all the merit derived from making offerings and serving the assembly of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
I universally pray that all sentient beings may attain even omniscience, and that all Buddha-dharmas may be completely perfected.
If one dedicates [the merit] toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* three times every day, O Great King!
All that you have done shall become pure, and your bodhisattva practices and so forth will likewise be fully accomplished.

Furthermore, Great King, the roots of goodness produced by the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* yield immeasurable rewards; whether born among humans or in the heavens, one shall always attain the most supreme excellence in every place.
And you, Great King, act in this same way, which is truly vast.
Furthermore, Great King!
The mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*) is most supreme and most excellent; if one's practice is also genuine, one will be able to accomplish the fruit of great enlightenment.
As stated in the *Abhayarājadharma-paripṛcchā-sūtra*:
"The merit generated by the arousal of the bodhicitta is as vast and supreme as the realm of space, being without end."

Even if someone were to offer as many precious jewels as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, filling Buddha-fields equal in number to those grains, as an offering to the World-Honored One; and if another person were able to join their palms with utmost sincerity and give rise to the thought of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* even once—the latter’s merit would surpass the former’s merit beyond all calculation.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"O son of good family!
From the bodhicitta arise all Buddha-dharmas, which are vast, supreme, and magnificent."
The bodhicitta is of two kinds: first, the aspirational mind; second, the engaged mind.
Furthermore, that sutra states:
"O son of good family!"
That which is most difficult for all sentient beings to attain is what is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If one extensively gives rise to practice and vows, one will immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and abide therein manifest before oneself, universally bringing benefit to the entire world.
"Good son!

When I attained Buddhahood, it was by means of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), mounting the mind of the original vow, and subsequently encompassing all subsequent practices within those previously generated practices, thereby forming the mind of the stages (*avasthā-citta*)."
Therefore, when the power of one's practice and vows is fully established, one will obtain the presence and guidance of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and abandon all unreal objective appearances.

Just as the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī generated the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta) before King Vastradatta, so too, having thus generated the mind of enlightenment, the bodhisattva personally practices the sublime conduct associated with the perfections (pāramitās), such as generosity and the rest.
If a person cannot discipline themselves, how can they discipline others?
Therefore, one should know that if a bodhisattva does not personally cultivate these practices, how could they attain the fruit of great enlightenment?
Furthermore, as the *Gajapati-sūtra* states:
"Bodhisattvas attain awakening because their practices are real, not because their practices are unreal."
As it is said in the *Samādhirāja Sūtra*:
"O youth! Since I have attained reality through my practice, you, O youth, should train in this very way."
Why is this? Young man,
if one’s practice is true, then it is not difficult to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

If one were to extensively analyze all such practices performed by a bodhisattva—such as the ten pāramitās, the four immeasurables, and the four means of attraction—as they are explained in the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*, and other scriptures.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of training: namely, mundane and supramundane.
What is mundane training?
It refers to skills, crafts, and the like.
What is supramundane training?
It refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and so forth.
What else is there?
This refers to all activities performed for the benefit of sentient beings.
In this regard, one should know that the conduct of bodhisattvas, stated in brief, consists of wisdom and skillful means; these two dharmas must not be allowed to diminish.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"For a bodhisattva, wisdom without skillful means is bondage; wisdom with skillful means is liberation.
Skillful means without wisdom is bondage; skillful means with wisdom is liberation."
Furthermore, as the *Gajapati-sūtra* states:

"In brief, there are two kinds of paths for all bodhisattvas; if they are fully endowed with these two paths, bodhisattvas will be able to swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)."
What are these two? They are wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*).

If one is separated from the *prajñāpāramitā*, how could one, while practicing the various *pāramitās* and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), be able to purify the Buddha-fields, attain great wealth and sovereignty, mature sentient beings, perform various transformative deeds, and universally encompass all dharmas through skillful means?
Therefore, this wisdom and that skillful means possess a non-erroneous nature and serve as the cause for discernment.
By virtue of this cause, correct skillful means arises.

Regarding all phenomena as they have been taught, one gives rise to non-erroneous contemplation and discernment, thereby being able to ultimately bring benefit and happiness to oneself and others, and enabling afflictions not to arise.
It is just as various poisons are neutralized by mantras.
Furthermore, this sutra states that wisdom encompasses skillful means; this refers to wisdom with conceptual differentiation (*savikalpa-jñāna*).
Moreover, as the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra* says:
What is skillful means? It is the gathering together of all phenomena.
What is wisdom?
This refers to the excellence of non-disruption regarding all phenomena.
Such wisdom and skillful means—these two types—pervade all stages and are practiced at all times, never allowing them to diminish therein.
All Bodhisattvas of the ten stages practice the ten pāramitās and, furthermore, engage in extensive practices as described at length in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
All Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage arise from and abide in the Buddha’s majestic deportment through the practice of resting in composure.
That sūtra states:

"Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should abide by the power of the roots of goodness sustained by the great vows previously generated; from this very dharma-gate, the World-Honored Buddhas also flow forth the perfection of great wisdom and all their enlightened activities."
This is precisely the gate of supreme patience, through which all Buddha-dharmas are gathered.
Furthermore, son of good family,
one should not engage in such rising, sitting, resting, or walking.

The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, the various supernormal knowledges, and all other Buddha-dharmas that I have attained—you do not yet possess these; you should therefore arouse diligence and practice in accordance with the generation of various aspirational prayers.
Therefore, you should not abandon this gate of patience.
Son of good family!

Have you not observed how ordinary, foolish worldlings accumulate various afflictions and give rise to various modes of seeking in an uninterrupted succession? How then can you wish to bring such activities to rest?
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should know that the dharma-nature of all phenomena abides eternally by itself.
Because the dharma-nature abides eternally, the Tathāgata is unborn.
Because the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not fully understand that all phenomena are non-conceptual and unarisen, the Tathāgata appears in the world through skillful means.
Furthermore, son of good family!

You see my body as immeasurable, my wisdom as immeasurable, the Buddha-fields as immeasurable, my halo as immeasurable, the gateways of manifesting wisdom as immeasurable, and my purity as immeasurable—such are these vast and great dharmas. Therefore, you should ride upon the practice of your original vow and constantly contemplate the benefit of sentient beings; thus, you shall attain such inconceivable gateways of wisdom.
Because the modes of practice described in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* contradict those in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
That sūtra states:
"O Mañjuśrī!"
If a person should give rise to disparagement toward the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, although that person utters words of slander, they will nonetheless attain purity as I have described.
In this regard, both principle and phenomenon are not in contradiction.
As stated in the *Gajapati-sūtra*, the Buddha said:
"Maitreya!
For the sake of awakening, all bodhisattvas accumulate the six pāramitās."
There may be some deluded person who speaks thus:
"The *prajñāpāramitā* is the training of a bodhisattva; why then train further in the other *pāramitās*?"
Or perhaps, having heard this, they might develop an intention to abandon the skillful means and the other perfections.
Maitreya, what do you think?
"Just as the King of Kāśi took his own flesh to save the pigeon—
was that king perhaps foolish? Maitreya replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said,
“Maitreya!”
"When I was practicing the bodhisattva path, did the roots of virtue associated with the extensive cultivation of the six pāramitās fail to bring benefit?
Maitreya replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“It is so, Maitreya!”
Just as you have accumulated the various pāramitās, such as generosity, throughout sixty kalpas, so too have you accumulated the prajñāpāramitā throughout sixty kalpas.
The detailed explanation of the practice therein should be understood.

Furthermore, regarding this matter, it is as stated in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi Sūtra*:
All forms of omniscient wisdom have compassion as their root.
From compassion arises the great bodhicitta, and from that, various skillful means are initiated; therefore, bodhisattvas always practice these two at all times.

All the vast fruits of retribution—such as the manifestation of bodies, lands, and the physical characteristics of retinues through skillful means like generosity—are fully accomplished by virtue of these two types of gathering.
This is just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not abide in nirvana, but rather causes all beings to give rise to right wisdom so that they may universally sever all inversions.
Furthermore, one does not abide in saṃsāra because saṃsāra arises from the occurrence of perversions; therefore, the World-Honored One has attained non-abiding nirvāṇa.

Moreover, it should be known that regarding the respective domains of wisdom and skillful means, one should distance oneself from the two extremes of common characteristics and slanderous denial; by being free from these two extremes, one attains unimpeded conduct in the middle way.

Regarding what is called "the side of common characteristics and the side of deprecation": wisdom is free from the side of common characteristics, and skillful means is free from the side of deprecation;
it is thus within this context. As stated in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"If one is fully endowed with the physical body of the marks and signs, one can cause those who behold it to give rise to a superior intention."
If one contemplates the Dharma-body within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one will be unable to give rise to the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Furthermore, it is said that wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*) give birth to all Tathāgatas and are able to cause others to give rise to pure faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*).
Thus it should be understood.
Furthermore, there is this saying:
"Just as worldly dharmas should be thoroughly understood, even dharmas should be relinquished, let alone non-dharmas, because one must be free from grasping at signs."

Those various inverted attachments and clingings of the mind are severed; because they have been severed, this is called the truly supreme intention (*adhyāśaya*), and one should not give rise to a mind of fixed certainty or reliance regarding those activities performed.
It is also as it has been said:
"Among all dharmas, there is neither that which can be grasped nor that which can be relinquished, because those dharmas of grasping and relinquishing cannot be found.
Or, as some have said:
Practices such as giving produce the fruits of birth and death.

How is this so? It means that when one practices giving and other virtues apart from wisdom, one becomes satisfied with attaining only a small portion of merit, gives rise to a mind of fierce exertion, and further conceives the notion that these are superior, preeminent roots of goodness.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"All dharmas should proceed in conjunction with both wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*).
If practices such as giving are embraced by wisdom, they are then designated by the name 'pāramitā'; otherwise, they are not the purification of giving and the other perfections."

In this regard, it should be understood that if one abides in samādhi and is able to give rise to various forms of wisdom (*prajñā*), the application of focused attention constitutes their collective function.

That is to say, by first giving rise to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and correctly upholding the meaning of one's own school’s tenets, the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is subsequently able to arise.

Thereupon, within the wisdom of reflection, one contemplates the meaning as it truly is; that which is thus contemplated is determined to be real, without any other element of error, unreality, or perversion.
By observing in this way, doubt ceases and right knowledge arises, leading to cultivation in accordance with reality.
Just as the various non-Buddhist teachers speak of the doctrine of no-self, one should contemplate and examine this: there must be a true cause for attaining the fruit of nirvana;
anything other than this is merely the conceptualization of eternal causes by non-Buddhists, which does not lead to tranquility.

Therefore, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and other scriptures state that within the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*), after one has investigated according to the principle, one should observe that although all things possess a real intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that intrinsic characteristic does not arise within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Thus, what is taught in the Āgamas is definitively consistent with this.
As stated in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"Non-arising is the reality; that which is unreal is called a distinct phenomenon."
All such things accord with the non-arising of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); this is called the reality.
Furthermore, the non-arising of the ultimate is itself not non-arising; all that is practiced therein has the nature of the past.
In this regard, it is further said:
"O son of good family!

The two dharmas of arising and ceasing are ultimately all worldly attachments. Therefore, the Buddha, the Greatly Compassionate One, wishing to awaken the world so that they might abandon all conditioned activities, taught that regarding arising, ceasing, and so forth, there is ultimately not even the slightest dharma that can arise."
Furthermore, the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* states:
"What is arising?
What is ceasing?"
Answer:
Non-arising is called arising; non-ceasing is called ceasing.
Furthermore, it is said herein:

The gate of the letter A signifies that all phenomena are free from arising and ceasing; this is the gate of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of all phenomena, established through the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
The *Āryasatyadvaya-sūtra* states:
"If there is equality in non-arising, one attains the equality of all phenomena."
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: “Subhūti!

Form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, and so on up to consciousness, which is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness; they are established as being empty of their own characteristics.”
The *Gaja-pāda-sūtra* states:
"The nature of all things cannot be found to arise.
Within this nature of non-arising, the deluded cling to the existence of arising."
The *Pitṛputrasamāgama-sūtra* states:
"All those phenomena are entirely equal, and the three times are likewise equal.
All past phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, and even all present phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature."
Thus, in summary, one should investigate the meaning of the "corresponding firmness" found in those Āgamas; otherwise, if there were a cause different from this, it could not be established.
Having investigated this through correct reasoning and definitive analysis, to state it briefly: regarding the nature of all births, some say they have a cause, while others say they are causeless.
One should know them as they truly are: neither do they have a cause, nor are they without a cause.
What is the meaning of this?
If the nature of the cause is relinquished, this differentiated nature might be manifested as real; it is not without a cause.
When a phenomenon arises, since all natures pervade all places, how could it not exist?
When those [factors] lack intrinsic nature, they are either undifferentiated, or even at the time of their arising, there is no attainment;
thus they do not possess a cause. To state it generally: they do not attain combination through being causeless, nor do they attain combination through having a cause.
Regarding what has been stated thus: if one conceives of a self, this is precisely the grasping at permanence held by the non-Buddhists;

they maintain that [the self] arises without an intrinsic nature, yet is capable of giving rise to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and it is for the purpose of demonstrating this that [the teaching] is shown.
If the nature of all causes is destroyed, how could conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise?
This is because they would have abandoned what is not in accordance with reality (*ayoniśas*).
Furthermore, the "self" (*ātman*) and so forth as asserted by non-Buddhists do not possess an inherent power capable of maintaining a non-abandoning nature toward other distinct phenomena.
Having grasped at a permanent nature, one is unable to perform acts of benefit for others.
If there is no benefit, one turns away from the corresponding Dharma.

In this regard, it should be understood that all the power and capacity of the "self" and so forth as they are grasped are ultimately empty, like the son of a barren woman; they lack intrinsic nature and cannot achieve anything in the performance of tasks.
Whatever actions they may perform lack real power and efficacy.
Furthermore, if there were neither action nor combination, and as with all things that arise following an action, they would necessarily exist at a later time.
If there is a capacity for power, then that very capacity follows its own nature and thus achieves the union of the activities produced as previously described.
Or, if it does not follow [that nature], then as previously stated, it lacks self-nature; being of an impermanent causal nature, it certainly cannot achieve union.
Therefore, among all that is impermanent, not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended.
The intended meaning here is as the Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!"

The unreal common characteristic refers to that which is called space, cessation, nirvāṇa, and the absence of an agent; it is the common characteristic of being without intrinsic nature and without grasping. Therefore, while impermanence and so forth arise, these do not coalesce, yet they are also not non-impermanent.

Just as in the nature of the two entities of past and future, there is no arising through which they could attain conjunction, for in their case, the causal nature that would allow such conjunction does not persist.
Even if simultaneous arising were associated with something, it is not the case that the self-nature of an entity produced by a simultaneous cause can be determined.
When observed simultaneously, it likewise lacks an established nature.
When observed at different times, it is not [observed] at different times.
If one observes within the conditions during that time, that too is unarisen and unreal.
If there were anything produced in the past through a combination of conditions, it would neither be a condition nor a production; thus, all such "selves" likewise lack conditions.
Furthermore, all moments do not enter into one another within a single moment, for the dimensions of eons and moments do not combine.
Just as when various atoms aggregate and coalesce into a mass, there is not even an atom's worth of a self within them that can undergo such combination.
Likewise, within a single part of such a mass, the nature of those momentary aggregates does not combine; they cannot arise of themselves, nor do they possess causal parts.
If one were to take up the nature of those parts within this [self], it would contradict the notion that the self is its own creator, and there would be no duality [of the self].
If there were a dual nature, then two kinds of faults would follow.
This is the general explanation.
Therefore, all that arises conventionally and possesses the nature of being apprehended is, in fact, without arising within the context of ultimate truth.
This teaching does not contradict the *Āgamas* and other such scriptures.
As the Buddha has said:
"All that possesses the nature of arising is called the conventional; in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), arising has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one gives rise to doubt regarding this absence of intrinsic nature, that is precisely the actual arising of the conventional mind.
What has been taught according to reason is the true and supreme intention of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Just as with the nature of rice stalks and the like—whether characterized by self-nature or other-nature—it is taught that they arise without a cause within these two categories.
This point should be set aside; herein, one ought to investigate according to reason.

If form and the formless possess those two natures—just as in the case of a jar or similar objects—their subtle particles do not destroy the nature of form, yet within their prior state, they are not of a single nature.
If there were anything destroyed within the preceding state, that [state] would not be established.
Furthermore, within an aggregation of atoms, there is neither a single nature nor a manifold nature; since those natures of unity and multiplicity are absent, how could there be an intrinsic nature?
If there is no intrinsic nature, this is the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
This meaning should be understood as being like the forms and the nature of form perceived within a dream;
this is what the Buddha has taught.
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Suppose a great elephant were reduced to atoms; if one examines those atomic characteristics according to reason, the nature of its form is found to be truly without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."

Furthermore, just as the various forms within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), such as blue and so forth, possess resistance yet lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too, ultimately, that which is non-form exists outside of consciousness.
This meaning should be understood.
As the Blessed One has said:
"There are no external forms; they are manifestations of one's own mind.

Those various external color-forms, such as blue and so forth, are in reality without resistance or obstruction; likewise, the characteristics of grasping and rejecting are also without resistance or obstruction. They do not correspond to a single nature, nor do they correspond to a manifold nature, for singularity and multiplicity are mutually exclusive.
What is meant by "not being of a single nature"?
Because it is of the nature of a single aggregate of form, it is not produced from a single [cause].
The meaning of "not being of a manifold nature" should likewise be understood.
In this context, one examines that all material forms lack substantiality in their own-being, and therefore possess no resistance.
That consciousness, too, is not real. Why is this?
The self-characteristic of consciousness is devoid [of intrinsic nature]; it is not said that form exists apart from consciousness.
Furthermore, the various self-characteristics of consciousness are unreal.
Because of this, consciousness is said to be unreal; therefore, the Buddha taught that consciousness is like a magical illusion.

Thus, in summary, whether it be a single nature or multiple natures, all natures are empty of intrinsic nature; in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), all natures are unreal—this meaning is certain.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
"For example, an image seen within a mirror is neither of the same nature nor of a different nature.
When observed in this way, its nature does not exist."
Why is this? Because it is free from the nature of identity and difference, and because it is not attached to the nature of identity and difference. Some may say:
The wise observe that intrinsic nature is truly unobtainable, for herein it cannot be explicitly described as being without intrinsic nature.

When one investigates all such statements in accordance with reason, this is the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); having become certain of reality as it is, this meaning is established.
From this, the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) shall arise;
yet, without hearing [the Dharma] and so forth, the wisdom of cultivation cannot be accomplished.
As it is said in the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*:
Those who practice correctly possess the light of wisdom; that which arises from the intermediate state remains unimpaired in its correctness.
Through wisdom, all that is cultivated arises and achieves accomplishment. It is like the earth filled with impurities: how could anything that grows therein truly flourish?
The same applies to all forms of cultivation: within the true nature that is the fruit of clear wisdom, one proceeds from principle according to principle.
As stated in the *Samādhirāja Sūtra*:
"If a person gives rise to various kinds of seeking, the mind so arisen will have attachments and dependencies."

Therefore, if one wishes to realize that true wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), one should first cultivate the sublime dharma associated with *śamatha*, causing the mind to abide peacefully like still water.
If the mind is in motion, it is not *śamatha*; it cannot maintain itself and abide.
As the Buddha has said, one who abides in a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) is able to know things as they truly are.
If one is in a state of distracted mind, this [equanimity] is not associated with it.

Therefore, when practicing śamatha, one should abide in impartial equanimity regarding all that is attained and all that is desired; within that essence, suffering and the like are entirely dispelled.
Abiding securely in pure ethical discipline and initiating diligence, one swiftly attains accomplishment;
it is thus in this regard. As stated in the *Saṃyuktavimokṣa-sūtra*:
"First, one cultivates superior practices such as generosity; next, one maintains pure ethical discipline; and thereafter, one dwells in the practice of śamatha."

If one wishes to abide in this śamatha, one should, according to the various stages, first take refuge in and repent before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and then rejoice in their merits. Next, one should give rise to great compassion, forming the intention to rescue and deliver all beings throughout the world. Seated cross-legged upon a stable seat, with the body held straight and upright, one should manifest clear mindfulness and bring forth the samādhi that corresponds to the present moment.

From the initial stage of focused attention and appropriate observation, up to the various types of objects of focus and so forth, one should universally gather and collect them all, binding the mind in tranquil abiding.
Furthermore, within the two categories of the form and formless realms, one should abandon the fault of distraction.

By bringing together those associated mental objects and giving rise to superior attention (*manasikāra*), one attains purification without making any conceptual distinctions regarding all phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
All the detailed explanations regarding the objects and modes of activity are as set forth in the eighteenth chapter, the *Saṃyukta-vimukti*, of the *Saṃyuktāgama*.

All the activities of the Blessed One for gathering sentient beings, including the analysis of form and so forth, as well as the analysis of all phenomena in their abbreviated, intermediate, and extensive modes, are as explained in the Abhidharma and other treatises.
The intention here is that, having contemplated those objects, one should abandon faults and fully withdraw [the mind], causing the mental continuum to progress and cultivate further excellence.
Should thoughts of desire or the like arise, at that time one should practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha*) and so forth.
Once one has attained stillness, one should again give rise to a superior and progressive mind beyond that previous state.
The contemplative aspects of such practices as the meditation on impurity are omitted here for fear of prolixity.

If, however, the mind is unable to progress toward a superior state and fails to give rise to a superior resolve, this too is a fault of distraction; at that time, one should contemplate the virtues of samādhi to generate a superior resolve, whereby one will be able to cease that lack of superior resolve.
If at any time dullness or drowsiness arises, one should contemplate the qualities of the Buddha and other such objects that inspire supreme joy; these will cause them to subside.
Furthermore, when one thus firmly holds the object of focus as appropriate and does not allow it to scatter, one attains meditative union (*yoga*).

Furthermore, whenever the preceding mind is characterized by attachment, delight, or joy, and a subsequent mind arises that is agitated or haughty, at that time one should practice the contemplation of impermanence and so forth.

To speak of this in general terms: within the object of focus, one should cause the mind to be free from movement, remaining concentrated and tranquil, detached from states of agitation and depression. Through such equanimous practice, the mind attains purity, and one completely abandons the causes of distraction and the like that give rise to them.
If there is any genuine movement of the mind in its activity, that mind is distracted.

If there is no such movement within the object of focus, one then attains the desired application of the superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*); at that time, one should know that *śamatha* has been accomplished.

One should understand that such characteristics as these are the common features of all śamatha; that is, the intrinsic nature within one-pointedness of mind, wherein the object of focus for that śamatha is thus determined.
Regarding these methods of śamatha, the Buddha taught them in such sūtras as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, it should be understood that there are nine methods for cultivating śamatha:

first, removal; second, thorough removal; third, removal by way of stages; fourth, proximate removal; fifth, subduing; sixth, cessation; seventh, proximate cessation; eighth, that which is performed with single-mindedness; and ninth, knowing cessation.
What are these nine modes of practice? They are as follows:
"pervasive removal" (vyapakarṣa) refers to binding the mind to the object of focus throughout these nine factors; this is what constitutes pervasive removal.
To proceed in a continuous stream toward the object of focus is "removal by stages.
To bring forth and completely subdue all forms of distraction is "near removal.
Once distraction has been abandoned, to further surpass the previous stage by universally removing the object of focus is "subjugation."
When craving arises, it is suppressed; therefore, it is called "stopping" (śamatha).
When the fault of distraction manifests, one does not give rise to it, but rather stops it through a superior intention; this is "near-stopping" (upaśama).
If dullness, sleep, and so forth arise, one should swiftly dispel them; this is what must be done exclusively.

Once one has attained non-distraction regarding the object of focus, one then concentrates to attain *śamatha*. Having attained that *śamatha*, the mind abides in equanimity (*upekṣā*); this is known as knowing *śamatha*.
These points are as taught by the noble Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Furthermore, it should be known that when practicing any samādhi, there are six kinds of faults:
first, laziness; second, loss of the object of focus; third, laxity; fourth, excitation; fifth, lack of alertness; and sixth, over-alertness.
When these six faults arise, one should give rise to eight types of formative acts (*saṃskāra*) as antidotes.
What are the eight? First, faith; second, aspiration; third, diligence; fourth, pliancy; fifth, mindfulness; sixth, clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*); seventh, volition; and eighth, equanimity.
What are the characteristics of these counteractive practices?
They are the four dharmas beginning with faith, which serve as antidotes to indolence.
The intended meaning here is that within the qualities of samādhi, one must possess the characteristic of superior, compliant faith.
One who is associated with that [practice] gives rise to superior aspiration; at the time of aspiring, one initiates the practice of vigor.
The vigor thus initiated brings forth physical and mental fortitude, followed by pliancy (praśrabdhi); therefore, it serves as an antidote.
One should understand that mindfulness is the remedy for the loss of the object of focus.

Correct awareness (*saṃprajanya*) is the remedy for mental dullness and agitation; that is to say, by giving rise to correct observation through correct awareness, one can cause the two states of high and low to subside, and therefore it serves as the remedy.
It should be understood that the meaning of "counteracting through reflection" is non-arousal.

As for "counteracting through equanimity," once the aforementioned fluctuations of high and low have been stilled, the mind abides in rectitude; thus, there is no further arousal, and this constitutes the counteraction.

Once these eight formative forces of abandonment have counteracted the six types of faults, the activities of the supreme samādhi are accomplished, and the merit of the bases of psychic power arises therefrom.
As stated in various sūtras, if one possesses the eight formative forces of abandonment (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*), one is able to give rise to the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).
When the supreme task of one-pointedness of mind attains correct correspondence, one is then able to enter the gateways of meditative concentration and liberation, and fulfill all supreme qualities.

Furthermore, herein the sequence for practicing those various dhyānas should be as follows: if one attains the joy and bliss born of detachment from sensual desire, with internal purity and abiding in right application, accompanied by directed thought and sustained investigation, this is the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, that which is without vitarka and possesses only vicāra is called the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
When one has become detached from craving for the level of the first dhyāna, the state of abiding in mental purity accompanied by joy and bliss is the second dhyāna.
When one has become detached from craving for the stage of the second dhyāna, and dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, this is the third dhyāna-concentration.
When one has become detached from craving for the stage of the third dhyāna, and dwells in equanimity associated with mindfulness, this is the fourth dhyāna-concentration.
All formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and so forth should be understood as being associated with such practices.

Within these, the characteristics of the objects of focus (*ālambana*) should be distinguished according to their respective natures. One should cause the mind to become firm within the object of focus, observing it with wisdom in accordance with reality; from this, the light of knowledge arises, destroying the seeds of ignorance, and one ultimately attains cessation, which is true meditative union (*samprayoga*).
Anything other than this is merely that practiced by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); it is not authentic *samādhi* and cannot sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As stated in various sūtras, whenever one is practicing samādhi correctly, if the notion of a self arises, this immediately gives rise to afflictions once again.
At that time, the mind should abide like still water, entering into the contemplative practice associated with samādhi.
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, to summarize briefly: the practice of observing with right wisdom consists solely in abiding in the stillness of mind-only, without external conceptualization.
If one abides in the object-condition of True Suchness (*tathatā*), this mind should transcend [the state of being a subject].
If the mind has already passed beyond [objects], it should likewise pass through that which is without resistance (*apratigha*).

To abide in accordance with that which is without resistance is the contemplation of the Mahāyāna; that state of non-awakening is supreme tranquility, namely the non-resistant contemplation of the wisdom of supreme selflessness.
The intended meaning here is that, through observing reality as it is, one realizes that there are necessarily no dharmas of form apart from the mind; this is precisely the supreme practice of yoga.
If this is so, how can consciousness and form be different?
If they were not different, would consciousness also possess the quality of resistance? No;
for what is seen during the state of a dream is unreal. Therefore, when one investigates thoroughly according to reality outside of consciousness, not even an atom's worth of form can be apprehended.

Because [external objects] cannot be apprehended, thus consciousness-only is established; no external referents whatsoever can exist, for the mind alone abides in tranquility, free from external conceptualization.

In the process of investigation, because one is free from material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), that which is characterized by apprehension is ultimately non-apprehensible; therefore, one should contemplate all material phenomena as being formless (*arūpa*).
If that is merely mind, there is no real grasper nor any grasped; the nature of these two graspings is truly unobtainable.
Because it is free from grasping and abandoning, the mind itself is non-dual; thus, through such investigation, even the appearance of duality is absent.

Within the objective support of suchness, this mind also transcends, and those grasped characteristics likewise transcend; when these two are without mutual obstruction, one abides in non-dual wisdom according to the reality of things as they are.

Since what is called "mind-only" has already transcended duality and is free from obstruction, wisdom itself should also be detached from it; therefore, within self-nature and other-nature, no nature of arising can be found.
Upon careful investigation, one finds that the natures of all sentient beings are likewise not composite; both grasping and rejecting, being unreal natures, should be entirely abandoned.
One should know that all objective natures and all forms of attachment must be relinquished within non-dual wisdom.

If one abides thus within non-obstructive, non-dual wisdom, one realizes all phenomena as they truly are—devoid of intrinsic nature—and thereby enters the supreme true nature and the gate of non-conceptual samādhi.

Furthermore, if one dwells in correspondence with this non-obstructive, non-dual wisdom, that is precisely dwelling within the supreme true nature; it is the vision of the Mahāyāna, and in this way, one also perceives the supreme true nature.
Because one perceives the supreme true nature, one views all phenomena as empty with the eye of wisdom; within the light of primordial cognition, they are all seen exactly as they are.
As stated in various sūtras, how does one perceive the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)?
This refers to the non-seeing of all phenomena.

In this context, what is called "non-seeing" is the ultimate non-seeing of the true intention (*abhiprāya*); it is not like the failure to see on the part of those born blind or those with eyes closed, which results from the absence of conditions or from a lack of mental attention.
It is not the case that those who possess the seeds of perversion are entirely unable to sever them.

Furthermore, just as when one enters the meditative attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and subsequently emerges from it, the grasping at existence arises once more, and because the mass of fundamental afflictions such as craving remains, one is not liberated.

The characteristics of the root afflictions, such as attachment and craving, which arise from clinging to the existence of intrinsic nature, are as explained in scriptures such as the *Āryasatyadvaya*.

Furthermore, it is said that entering the dharma-gate of non-conceptual dhāraṇī means that within the state of non-conceptual phenomena, one is free from signs such as form; by means of definitive wisdom, one perceives nothing to be attained within the formless and remains without mental engagement—this is the bliss of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is not like the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth, wherein one attends to and becomes detached from the phenomena of form and so on that are objects of grasping.

Therefore, it should be understood that regarding the characteristics of detachment through attention toward the aforementioned forms and so forth, if right wisdom is absent, one cannot sever the seeds of doubt and confusion.
For example, when fire exists in the world, all things are consumed by its flames.
How can one be free from the single factor of conceptual thought?
If all that is perverse is not stilled and brought under control.

From this one should know that, when the mind dwells firmly upon any object of focus within śamatha, the light of wisdom arises through investigation performed in accordance with reality; as clarity manifests and darkness is dispelled, wisdom is born and obscurations are extinguished.
Just as a person’s two eyes function without distinction according to their capacity, illuminating all states without difference;
so too does the radiance of wisdom emerge.
There is no nature of darkness within that radiance, for the two phenomena of light and darkness are mutually exclusive.
One should know that the state of being free from darkness within samādhi is likewise so.
If it were not thus, how could one abide in the state of one-pointedness of mind?
Therefore, if one understands reality as it is within samāhita, one will be able to accord exclusively with right wisdom; what is stated here is entirely without contradiction.
Furthermore, within *samāhita*, one should observe with wisdom that there is no appearance of form whatsoever, and that nothing at all can be apprehended among all phenomena.

Within those various states of associated factors, there is no further progression and no awakening; whether regarding oneself or others, one sees them all as being without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), such that all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding the characteristics of existence and non-existence is completely stilled.

In this way, one attains correspondence within the signless nature (*animitta*) observed by right wisdom; no mental discrimination can establish anything therein, and even that very absence of nature (*abhāva*) cannot be apprehended.
If, within this, one were to claim that there is a nature that can be perceived, such a view should be ceased.
Once it has been thus ceased, if one were to engage in conceptual proliferation regarding the absence of nature, that too would not be correct.

Even if one were to posit that existence possesses a nature corresponding to the three times, when observed with the eye of wisdom as being without marks and without attainment, how could there even be any "stopping"?
As for the meaning of reality (*yathārtha*), one should not differentiate between existence and non-existence; nor should one differentiate between oneness and difference.

In this regard, if one is free from the two conceptual discriminations of existence and non-existence, one is able to fully illuminate and penetrate the emptiness of all such discriminations; even that which illuminates and the nature of that which is illuminated are themselves non-existent. In this way, one attains the supreme and most excellent correspondence with non-discrimination.

In this context, if one abides in such a state of correspondence, all conceptual constructions can be completely severed, and both the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations can likewise be eliminated.
Within that nature of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which is neither arising nor ceasing, the root of the inversion of nature is entirely eliminated.

As stated in such sūtras as the *Āryasatyadvaya*, when all conceptualizations of the nature of things are severed and exhausted through such corresponding practice, the very self-nature of the ignorance that constitutes the inversion of nature—the root of the afflictive hindrances—is itself severed.
Once that root has been severed, all afflictive obstructions can be completely eliminated.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Āryasatyadvaya-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī was asked:
"How can one achieve the subduing of the afflictions?"
"How can one thoroughly understand afflictions?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"In the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), they are ultimately unarisen."

Within the nature of non-arising of all those phenomena, all conventionalities are unreal and inverted; one should therefore cease all conceptualization and discrimination arising from the notion of intrinsic natures and so forth.

If that conceptualization and discrimination do not cease, there is the characteristic of a self and commonality; once the characteristic of a self and commonality exists, various views arise, and when views arise, afflictions immediately manifest.
"O Son of Heaven!
If one can thoroughly understand that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), then the ultimate truth possesses ten kinds of non-perversion."

If, within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), there is no inversion, then there is no conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If there is no conceptual construction, one attains correspondence with cessation (*nirodha*). If one corresponds with cessation, then the common characteristics of self and others cannot be apprehended. Since the common characteristics of self and others cannot be apprehended, those various views cannot arise; even the view of nirvāṇa does not arise within the ultimate truth.
Because of this, all afflictions are ultimately subdued within the practice of non-arising.

O Son of Heaven, you should know that, within the unimpeded wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all afflictions are ultimately empty, ultimately signless, and ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature.
One who knows in this way understands the afflictions.
O Devaputra!
Just as a venomous snake is neutralized by a mantra, so too are the seeds of those afflictions.
The Devaputra asked again:
"What are the seeds of affliction?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"O Son of Heaven!

Within that ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) which is of the nature of absolute non-arising, when one gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding any phenomena, this itself becomes the seed of all afflictions (kleśa). From this, various types of perversions arise, and within these perversions, one is unable to penetrate and realize the truth."

Therefore, if one is able to sever all inversions regarding the phenomena to be abandoned, one will correctly determine and completely eliminate all cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); once the cognitive obstructions are severed, there is no further continuity.
For example, when the sunlight emerges, free from all clouds and veils, it illuminates everywhere without obstruction.
In the same way, the light of that wisdom is pure and illuminating; whether regarding form or mind, the intrinsic nature of all things is likewise so.

The true nature of all things is definitively and eternally abiding; for one who has truly realized, within the state of non-continuity, the reality of the nature of all things as it truly is—how could that nature of things be expressed by means of words?
Therefore, having understood all forms and the nature of all things exactly as they are described within those ultimate and conventional truths, one immediately attains omniscience.
The meanings of the severance of hindrances and so forth as thus explained constitute the supreme and most excellent path for realizing omniscience.
It is not the path of the śrāvakas and others; for those [paths] cannot exhaustively eliminate all perversions, nor can they correctly sever the two hindrances.
As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
"O Mahāmati!

Those śrāvakas give rise to distinct causes and become attached to them; having perceived phenomena, they grasp them as nirvāṇa and claim to have attained Buddhahood, yet they are unable to perceive the principle of dharma-nairātmya (the selflessness of phenomena)."
Mahāmati! This is not liberation.

Such śrāvakas have not truly attained deliverance through the realization of their own wisdom, yet they claim to have attained it; this is because their divergent views have undergone a transformation.
Yet that which they practice does not correspond to this, and the path they travel is not true liberation.
The World-Honored One teaches only the Dharma of the Single Vehicle; he does not teach the paths of the śrāvakas and others.
Those śrāvakas merely observe the absence of self within the aggregates, and what they attain is called the "selflessness of persons. This is not the case here;
one should observe that everything in the three realms is representation-only (vijñaptimātra).

If one claims that by asserting the existence of objects external to consciousness one attains selflessness, such a person will not enter into the selflessness of non-dual gnosis, because they seek entry through the nature of other-dependence (paratantra-svabhāva).
If one were to enter by means of another nature, that would not be the entry into the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
Furthermore, as it is said in the "Noble Supramundane Chapter" (*Āryalokottaraparivarta*) of this same sutra:
"Moreover, O Son of the Buddha, you should know that the triple world is mind-only; what appears is mind, and neither center nor periphery can be apprehended."
If one says there is a limit, then there is that which arises; if one says there is a middle, then there is that which abides. All such things are merely conceptualized characteristics.
If the mind is devoid of middle and extremes, it is therefore able to enter that non-dual wisdom; entering in this manner is true entry.
In this regard, a question is asked:
"If it is so, how do the various states of the associated factors arise?
The answer is:
By the power of that pure and supreme vow, the bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion and universally performs deeds for the benefit of sentient beings.
From that vow-power, there arise superior and sublime virtuous practices such as giving; these are born from true purity.

Furthermore, because of the Bodhisattva’s great compassion, as long as all sentient beings have not yet been able to fully enter the pure wisdom of the non-substantiality of all phenomena, the Bodhisattva continues to follow them through saṃsāra; yet, while remaining untainted by the faults of saṃsāra, how could he abide in that unawakened state of quiescent phenomena?
As a verse in a sutra says:
"Seeing within that which is without obstruction is the supreme wisdom of selflessness.

Therefore, if one speaks words of non-duality regarding the state of non-dual characteristics, this is the most excellent; it is the truly superior intention within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Within non-dual and unobstructed wisdom, there is ultimately no self and no intrinsic nature; thus, one attains correspondence with what is seen.
Whatever seeing exists therein is not a distinct or differentiated seeing; it is entirely free from conceptual construction and mental arousal, being wholly quiescent.
He asked again:
"If that is so, how can one give rise to the various associated formations?
He replied:
Otherwise,
if there were someone who held the view:
"That [conventional reality] truly cannot conform to the ultimate truth."
Why is this? Because within this there is no characteristic of a sovereign self that corresponds to mastery; how, then, could there be any "seeing"?

It is merely because, within the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti-dharma*), one conforms to the characteristics of objects such as form (*rūpa*) that, when wisdom arises, consciousness likewise conforms to worldly activity.

Therefore, it should be understood that when those who possess wisdom experience a profound resonance within their cognition, they speak of having "something seen"; yet this is not a truly existent characteristic such as a governing self.
When non-dual and unimpeded wisdom arises, one understands reality as it is, and is thus able to attain true vision within that wisdom.
It is not that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature within the ultimate truth while being definitively applicable to the conventional truth;
for if it were otherwise, this would be the narrow and inferior wisdom of ordinary beings.
As stated in the *Āryasatyadvaya-sūtra*:
"In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is ultimately no intrinsic nature; this should likewise be observed within the conventional path (*saṃvṛti-mārga*).
If it were otherwise, how could the various stages—the foolish worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*), śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas—be established?"
This means that because conventional reality is without cause and conventional reality is without arising.
However, this is not the case here; for within the path of conventional truth, one observes according to what is appropriate, whereas in ultimate truth, there is truly nothing that arises.
If there were anything to be apprehended within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it would be like a rabbit's horn and the like.
All conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛtidharma*) are like illusions, reflections, echoes, and so forth.
Because this is so, the nature of things (*dharmatā*) is not incompatible between conventional dependent origination and the ultimate truth.
He examines and investigates that which has no nature of alteration or change; it is thus in this regard.
One should know that all things in the world are like an illusion: the various afflictions and karmas are the causes of illusion, and the birth of sentient beings is the manifestation of illusion.
All corresponding practices of merit and wisdom are likewise causes of illusion, and such corresponding wisdom operates within illusion itself.
As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

"Subhūti! All śrāvakas are like transformations; pratyekabuddhas are like transformations; bodhisattvas are like transformations; tathāgatas are like transformations; afflictions are like transformations; and karma is like transformations."
Subhūti! For this reason, all dharmas are like transformations.
These various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such as these, as well as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), are all like illusory appearances.
Within that illusion, whatever is perceived is entirely unreal grasping.
If one can know it in this way, one is a practitioner who is in accord with reality.
If one clings to it as real and grasps at it, one is a foolish ordinary person.
What has been stated in this manner is indeed not contradictory.
As a verse in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* says:
"Just as the activities performed by a magician, And the liberation arising from an emanation,"
This is understood as previously explained: there is no attachment within the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya).
It is taught that the three realms of existence are like a transformation; this the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas fully know.
Having known this, they don the supreme armor and bring benefit to the world.
Within all such practices, one should contemplate their true nature.
As previously explained regarding śamatha, when states such as mental depression or excitation arise, one should contemplate that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
At that time, one should abandon mental engagements with high and low, and wisdom will achieve accomplishment.

The path practiced by those practitioners engaged in śamatha and vipaśyanā will then become fully complete, until they are able to give rise to the power of faith and understanding, abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi).
When one wishes to arise from meditation, one again contemplates that within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
and that the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) likewise abides in this manner.
As it is said in the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*:
How does a bodhisattva attain the principle of non-self?
Son of good family!
A bodhisattva should observe form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness with right wisdom.

When he observes in this way, the arising of form cannot be apprehended, its accumulation cannot be apprehended, and its cessation cannot be apprehended; likewise, for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, their arising, accumulation, or cessation are all unapprehendable.
Having realized the non-arising of phenomena within that ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one gives rise to the observation of wisdom and no longer has any grasping toward what is practiced.

Because of this, those who are ignorant and lack wisdom grasp at such things—which lack intrinsic nature—as having intrinsic nature; they grasp them with perversion. Consequently, the cycle of birth and death continues without end, and they experience manifold sufferings in the present without any respite.

The great compassion of a bodhisattva thus constantly gives rise to uninterrupted reflection and manifests in direct action; out of pity and for the benefit of others, they give rise to supreme vows and practices, just as I have practiced.
Having attained all-knowledge accordingly, one awakens to this dharmatā as it truly is, and thereafter makes offerings and praises to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others.
Having accomplished what was to be done, from the treasury of compassion within emptiness, there arises all meritorious conduct such as generosity.
As stated in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:

"If bodhisattvas manifest according to reality, it means that they transform the bliss of this samādhi of mine toward all sentient beings through great compassion; they manifest according to reality within all phenomena, acting for the benefit of all sentient beings."

When this great compassion is thus awakened, one immediately attains the perfection of all trainings—superior ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—and achieves *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In this regard, it should be understood that wisdom and skillful means constitute the supreme path of practice for all bodhisattvas; they do not sever conventional truth while manifesting ultimate truth.
If one does not sever conventional reality, one can take great compassion as the precursor and skillfully perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, remaining free from inversion.
This is precisely what is called being well-established in supramundane wisdom.
By means of this, one acts in accordance with skillful means (*upāya*).

While engaged in the practice of these various skillful means, one understands their illusory nature and remains free from inversion. Through supramundane knowledge, one skillfully cultivates the most excellent skillful means according to suchness (*tathatā*), thereby generating a courageous resolve within the context of the true meaning of reality and giving rise to supreme wisdom.
Once the bodhisattva has attained this wisdom and skillful means, they abide in the superior path of practice that accords with reality.
As stated in the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra*:
"Meditative concentration is inexhaustible, and it is able to give birth to both wisdom and skillful means."
One should know that what is produced therein is precisely the supreme path practiced by those who engage in yoga.
[From] the third fascicle of the *Extensive Explanation of the Bodhicitta-śāstra*, [it asks]: "How can the thorns of false conceptualization and the like be uprooted?"
Furthermore, how can one here abandon the seeds of doubt and confusion?
It means that within the meditative concentration of union, one observes those seeds as empty with the eye of wisdom, just as previously described.
If one were to attain [anything] within form and so forth by means of the characteristics that are attained, there would ultimately be nothing attained.
It is like a person who, being deluded, mistakes a rope for a snake; once wisdom realizes it, there is no difference [between the two].
The same principle applies to being free from doubt regarding form (*rūpa*).

Observing all objects with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), one sees that they are unreal and products of false and deluded conceptualization; it is like a person situated in a dark room who further closes the door, remaining entirely in darkness and seeing nothing at all.
Furthermore, it is like various objects placed inside a vessel such as a jar; because they are covered by a lid, they cannot be seen.

The meaning here is that although nothing is seen in a dark room or similar setting, one still cannot escape the conceptual grasping and attachment to the existence of form and other phenomena, even amidst doubt.
Because they are not separated [from grasping], although they have no views, they do not eliminate the fault of [continued] attachment.
For such people, how could their various minds of clinging ever be completely severed?

Therefore, one should, by means of samādhi, take up the extremely subtle and sharp sword of wisdom in hand and sever those seeds of false and deluded discrimination regarding thought, form, and so forth.
Because such reality is severed, it is like uprooting a tree and removing it entirely along with its roots; once the ground is rootless, it will no longer grow.
Once the seeds of false thinking have been severed, all faults will never arise again.
In this context, the meaning of severing hindrances and so forth constitutes the dharma-gate associated with śamatha and vipaśyanā; that is, the path traversed by the practitioner.
As the Blessed One said:
"This gateway of correspondence is the causal nature of non-conceptual, correct wisdom.
Therefore, a verse in the Sūtra says:
First abide securely in ethical discipline, then attain meditative concentration; having attained that concentration, one should cultivate wisdom.
When wisdom is purified, perfected, and luminous, its purity first arises from the fullness of ethical discipline.
